title: Internal Use Software (IUS)
description: Internal use software, built for general and administrative functions, qualifies only if it passes the four-part and high threshold of innovation tests.
summary: Internal use software (IUS) is software a U.S. taxpayer develops primarily for internal general and administrative functions—financial management, human resources, or support services. Under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(E) and Treasury Regulation 1.41-4(c)(6), IUS research qualifies for the federal R&D tax credit only if it passes the four-part test and the three-part high threshold of innovation test.

body.text: Internal use software (IUS) is software a U.S. taxpayer develops primarily for internal general and administrative functions—financial management, human resources, or support services. Under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(E) and Treasury Regulation 1.41-4(c)(6), IUS research qualifies for the federal R&D tax credit only if it passes the four-part test and the three-part high threshold of innovation test.

Internal Use Software (IUS) under United States federal research and development (R&D) tax credit law—governed by Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41) and Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6), promulgated via Treasury Decision 9786 (T.D. 9786, 81 FR 68306, effective October 4, 2016)—is defined as computer software developed by, or for the benefit of, a taxpayer primarily for the taxpayer's internal use in general and administrative (G&A) functions that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business. Under the statutory mandate of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(E), research activities with respect to IUS are statutorily excluded from "qualified research" unless those activities fall within an explicit statutory or regulatory exception or satisfy a heightened three-part regulatory standard known as the High-Threshold-of-Innovation (HTI) test in addition to the standard four-part qualified research test under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1). Pursuant to 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B), G&A functions are strictly confined to three operational categories: (1) financial management functions, (2) human resources management functions, and (3) support services functions that support the day-to-day operations of the taxpayer. Software not developed for use in these G&A functions—including software developed to be commercially sold, leased, licensed, or otherwise marketed to third parties, or software developed to enable a taxpayer to interact with third parties or to allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system—is classified as non-internal use software (Non-IUS) and is evaluated under the standard four-part test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) without regard to the HTI test.

items: Vendor Interaction and the Third-Party Exclusion (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(E) and Example 6): The regulation explicitly states that for purposes of the third-party interaction exception (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv)(B)), "third parties do not include any persons that use the software to support the general and administrative functions of the taxpayer". As illustrated in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(viii) Example 6, software enabling vendors to initiate functions or review data to support the taxpayer's inventory management or procurement remains pure IUS. Furthermore, even where qualifying third parties (such as retail customers) interact with a system that also performs G&A functions, the project is not pulled entirely out of IUS; rather, it is classified as Dual Function Software (DFS) under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(A) and is presumed to be IUS unless a discrete third-party subset is isolated (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B)) or the 25% safe harbor applies (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C)).

IRS Software Audit Guidelines Scope (I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) vs. § 41(d)(4)(E)): The IRS Audit Guidelines explicitly state in their footnotes that they do not address the internal-use software exclusion under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(E) or its applicable exceptions; instead, they evaluate the process of experimentation under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) across all software and designate specific non-experimental software activities—such as "Maintenance of Existing Software Applications/Products," "Software Application Configuration," rewriting an application in a new language, writing hardware device drivers to support new hardware, data cleansing/formatting, and bundling existing software products into suites—as "High Risk" activities that usually fail to constitute qualified research under I.R.C. § 41(d).

Financial Accounting Standards Modernization (FASB ASU 2025-06 Amending ASC 350-40): On September 18, 2025, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) issued Accounting Standards Update (ASU) 2025-06 (Targeted Improvements to the Accounting for Internal-Use Software), which removes all references to project development stages in ASC 350-40 (and supersedes ASC 350-50 by merging website development costs into ASC 350-40) and replaces them with a dual-condition recognition threshold (ASC 350-40-25-12 and 25-12A): capitalization begins only when management authorizes and commits to funding the software project and the "probable-to-complete recognition threshold" is met, which cannot occur while "significant development uncertainty" (such as unproven or novel technological innovations not yet resolved through coding and testing) remains unresolved. ASU 2025-06 is effective for annual reporting periods beginning after December 15, 2027, with early adoption permitted.

Tax Treatment of Domestic R&E Expenditures (IRC § 174A vs. IRC § 174): OBBBA also enacted transition options allowing taxpayers to deduct remaining unamortized 2022–2024 domestic R&E costs in 2025 (or over a two-year period in 2025 and 2026) and permitting eligible small businesses to apply § 174A retroactively by amending 2022–2024 returns.

body.text: Statutory and Regulatory Foundation of IUS Qualification
Context of the Credit: IRC Section 41, Section 174A, and Qualified Research

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a), the federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities (the R&D tax credit, originally enacted in 1981 and made permanent by the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015) equals the sum of three components: (1) 20% of the excess (if any) of the taxpayer's qualified research expenses (QREs) for the taxable year over the base amount, (2) 20% of basic research payments determined under 26 U.S.C. § 41(e)(1)(A), and (3) 20% of amounts paid or incurred by the taxpayer in carrying on any trade or business during the taxable year (including as contributions) to an energy research consortium for energy research. Alternatively, taxpayers may elect the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-9, which provides a 14% credit on so much of the taxpayer's QREs for the taxable year as exceeds 50% of the average QREs for the three taxable years preceding the taxable year for which the credit is being determined (with a special rule under § 41(c)(4)(B) where the taxpayer has no QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years).

Pursuant to 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1)–(3) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2, QREs comprise both in-house research expenses and contract research expenses paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer (where "in carrying on a trade or business" has the same meaning under § 41(b)(1) as under 26 U.S.C. § 162, except that under § 41(b)(4) the trade or business requirement is disregarded for in-house research expenses of startup ventures whose principal purpose is to use the research results in the active conduct of a future trade or business of the taxpayer or an aggregated § 41(f)(1) person). Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)–(d), in-house research expenses encompass three specific categories of direct expenditures. First, in-house research expenses include wages (as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a), or earned income as defined in § 401(c)(2) for self-employed individuals and owner-employees under § 401(c)(1), but excluding any amount taken into account in determining the work opportunity credit under 26 U.S.C. § 51(a)) paid or incurred to an employee for "qualified services"—consisting of engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research, or engaging in the direct supervision (first-line management) or direct support of research activities that constitute qualified research. If an employee performs both qualified and nonqualified services, wages are allocated based on the ratio of time spent on qualified services to overall time worked; however, under the "substantially all" rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2), if at least 80% of the services performed by an employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year consist of qualified services, then 100% of the services performed by that employee during the taxable year are treated as qualified services. Second, in-house research expenses include amounts paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research, defined in 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C) as any tangible property other than land, improvements to land, and property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1)–(2), expenditures for supplies or personal property that are indirect research expenditures or general and administrative expenses (including routine building utilities such as water, electricity, and natural gas, unless the taxpayer establishes additional extraordinary utility expenditures required by the special character of the qualified research) do not qualify as in-house research expenses. Third, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4), in-house research expenses include amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use (time-sharing) computers in the conduct of qualified research, provided three regulatory conditions are satisfied: the computer is owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, it is located off the taxpayer's premises, and the taxpayer is not the primary user of the computer (and under § 41(b)(2)(A), this provision does not apply to the extent the taxpayer or an aggregated § 41(f)(1) person receives or accrues any amount from any other person for the right to use substantially identical personal property).

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e), contract research expenses equal 65% of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer in carrying on a trade or business to any person other than an employee of the taxpayer for the performance on behalf of the taxpayer of qualified research or services that, if performed by employees of the taxpayer, would constitute qualified services. This statutory percentage increases to 75% for amounts paid or incurred to a qualified research consortium (a tax-exempt organization described in § 501(c)(3) or § 501(c)(6) organized and operated primarily to conduct scientific research that is not a private foundation, conducting research on behalf of the taxpayer and one or more unrelated taxpayers under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(C)) and to 100% for eligible energy research payments made to eligible small businesses (500 or fewer average employees), institutions of higher education (§ 3304(f)), or Federal laboratories under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(D). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3), contract research payments qualify only to the extent made pursuant to an agreement that: (1) is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, (2) provides that the research be performed on behalf of the taxpayer (meaning the taxpayer has a right to the research results, although exclusive rights are not required), and (3) requires the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful (if payment is contingent on the success of the research, it is considered paid for the product or result rather than the performance of research and is disqualified). Furthermore, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(4), if any contract research expenses paid or incurred during a taxable year are attributable to qualified research to be conducted after the close of that taxable year, those prepaid amounts are treated as paid or incurred during the period in which the qualified research is actually conducted.

To constitute "qualified research" under the general rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(1)–(2), research activities must be applied separately to each discrete business component (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A)—defined in § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer) and satisfy a mandatory four-part test:

items: Section 174 / 174A Eligibility Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i)): The research must be activity with respect to which expenditures may be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A (following the July 4, 2025 OBBBA statutory text update; 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i) continues to reference section 174 and § 1.174-2, requiring research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense).

Technological in Nature / Discovering Information Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)–(4)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature—meaning it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving a business component, or the appropriate design of a business component, and the process of experimentation used to discover such information fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii)–(iii), the taxpayer is not required to seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field, nor must the research succeed in developing the new or improved component, and the issuance of a utility patent by the Patent and Trademark Office (other than a design patent) is conclusive evidence that the taxpayer discovered technological information intended to eliminate uncertainty.

Business Component / Permitted Purpose Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(3); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii)): The application of the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer for a qualified purpose—specifically, a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component (§ 41(d)(3)(A)), and never relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors (§ 41(d)(3)(B)).

Process of Experimentation Test (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)): Substantially all—defined in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80% or more measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis—of the research activities with respect to the business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation (identifying technical uncertainty, identifying one or more alternatives to eliminate that uncertainty, and conducting an evaluative process such as modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error to evaluate those alternatives) for a qualified purpose. If a business component as a whole fails these requirements, the "shrinking-back rule" of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) directs that the requirements be applied to the most significant subset of elements of the business component until either a subset satisfies the requirements or the most basic element fails.

body.text: Economic Rationale and Analysis: As documented by the Tax Foundation, the economic justification for the federal R&D credit rests on the market-failure principle of positive externalities: private-sector R&D generates social returns across the wider economy that exceed the private financial returns captured by the investing enterprise, leading to market underprovision in the absence of a tax subsidy.
Evolution of IUS Rules: From Statutory Exclusion to Final Regulations (T.D. 9786)
The statutory exclusion governing internal use software is codified in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(E), which states verbatim:

"Except to the extent provided in regulations, any research with respect to computer software which is developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for internal use by the taxpayer, other than for use in— (i) an activity which constitutes qualified research (determined with regard to this subparagraph), or (ii) a production process with respect to which the requirements of paragraph (1) are met."

Following two decades of administrative controversy under earlier regulatory iterations—specifically the 2001 final regulations (T.D. 8930, 66 FR 280, Jan. 3, 2001), the 2001 proposed regulations (REG-112991-01, 66 FR 66362, Dec. 26, 2001), the 2004 Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (REG-153656-03, 69 FR 43, Jan. 2, 2004), and the 2015 notice of proposed rulemaking (REG-153656-03, 80 FR 2624, Jan. 20, 2015; IRB 2015-5)—the Treasury Department and the IRS published final regulations in Treasury Decision 9786 (T.D. 9786, 81 FR 68306, Oct. 4, 2016; 2016-42 I.R.B.), amending 26 CFR § 1.41-4.

Resolution of Effective and Applicability Date Conflict: In reviewing secondary practitioner commentary against primary regulatory text, a discrepancy appears between an EY Tax Alert (2016-1704), which stated that T.D. 9786 is "effective for tax years ending on or after October 4, 2016," and the codified Treasury Regulation (26 CFR § 1.41-4(e)), which carries controlling legal weight. Under the verbatim text of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(e) and the T.D. 9786 Preamble (81 FR 68306), the regulations became effective on October 4, 2016, and paragraph (c)(6) is "applicable for taxable years beginning on or after October 4, 2016". For transition periods, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(e) and the Preamble establish that for any taxable year that both ends on or after January 20, 2015 (the publication date of the 2015 proposed regulations, 80 FR 2624) and begins before October 4, 2016, the IRS will not challenge return positions consistent with either all of paragraph (c)(6) of the final regulations (T.D. 9786) or all of paragraph (c)(6) of the 2015 proposed regulations (IRB 2015-5). Additionally, the 2004 ANPRM (69 FR 43) was withdrawn effective for taxable years beginning on or after January 20, 2015; for taxable years ending before January 20, 2015, taxpayers could choose to follow either all IUS provisions in the 2001 final regulations (T.D. 8930, 66 FR 280) or all IUS provisions in the 2001 proposed regulations (REG-112991-01, 66 FR 66362).
Definitional Scope: What Constitutes Internal Use Software (IUS)
Software Developed Primarily for Internal Use and Related-Party Rules

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(A), except as otherwise provided in the dual function software rules of paragraph (c)(6)(vi), software is developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for the taxpayer's internal use if the software is developed for use in general and administrative (G&A) functions that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business. Similarly, software that the taxpayer develops primarily for a related party's internal use is considered internal use software, where a "related party" is defined as any corporation, trade or business, or other person treated as a single taxpayer with the taxpayer pursuant to the controlled-group and common-control aggregation rules of 26 U.S.C. § 41(f).

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(v) (Time and manner of determination), whether software is developed primarily for internal use or not developed primarily for internal use depends on the intent of the taxpayer and the facts and circumstances at the beginning of the software development. During the T.D. 9786 rulemaking, commenters noted that software development is iterative and requested that intent be evaluated at any point during development, as of the tax return filing date, or based on actual post-deployment usage. The Treasury Department and the IRS rejected those requests and retained the inception-date rule in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(v), explaining that requiring the determination at the beginning of software development aligns with Congressional intent that the research credit serve as an incentive to conduct qualifying research rather than an unanticipated reward after the fact. Under this rule, software is not considered IUS solely because it is used internally for purposes of testing prior to commercial sale, lease, or license.

Furthermore, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(v) establishes a symmetrical bifurcation rule for subsequent software improvements. If a taxpayer originally develops software primarily for internal use, but later makes improvements to the software with the intent to hold the improved software to be sold, leased, licensed, or otherwise marketed to third parties, or to interact with third parties or allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system using the improved software, those improvements are considered separate from the existing software and are not considered developed primarily for internal use. (This primary regulatory text in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(v) corrects a secondary consultancy blog claim in McGuire Sponsel, which stated that commercial improvements to original IUS must still pass the HTI test; under the controlling text of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(v), the subsequent commercial improvements are treated as a separate Non-IUS component evaluated under the standard four-part test.) Conversely, if a taxpayer originally develops software to be sold, leased, licensed, or otherwise marketed to third parties, or to interact with third parties or allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system, and later makes improvements to the software with the intent to use the software in G&A functions, those improvements are considered separate from the existing software and are classified as developed primarily for internal use. Similarly, for connectivity software—such as bridging software, integration software, or middleware that allows multiple processes running on one or more machines to interact across a network—T.D. 9786 does not create a standalone rule; instead, whether connectivity software is IUS or Non-IUS depends on the underlying function the software provides.
Explicit Limitation to General and Administrative (G&A) Functions

A foundational structural reform in T.D. 9786 is that software is classified as IUS only if it is developed for use in G&A functions (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(A) and (iv)). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B), G&A functions are limited to three enumerated categories: (1) Financial Management (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(1)), comprising functions that involve the financial management of the taxpayer and the supporting recordkeeping; (2) Human Resources Management (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(2)), comprising functions that manage the taxpayer's workforce; and (3) Support Services (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(3)), comprising other functions that support the day-to-day operations of the taxpayer.

Specifically, terms such as "procurement," "investments," "talent acquisition, performance analysis, continuous development, employee wellness," and "incident management, customer service" do not appear in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B).

cells: 1. Financial Management (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(1))
Functions that involve the financial management of the taxpayer and the supporting recordkeeping.

Accounts payable, accounts receivable, inventory management, budgeting, cash management, cost accounting, disbursements, economic analysis and forecasting, financial reporting, finance, fixed asset accounting, general ledger bookkeeping, internal audit, management accounting, risk management, strategic business planning, and tax.
2. Human Resources Management (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(2))
Functions that manage the taxpayer's workforce.
Recruiting, hiring, training, assigning personnel, and maintaining personnel records, payroll, and benefits.
3. Support Services (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(3))
Other functions that support the day-to-day operations of the taxpayer.

Data processing, facility services (e.g., grounds keeping, housekeeping, janitorial, and logistics), graphic services, marketing, legal services, government compliance services, printing and publication services, and security services (e.g., video surveillance and physical asset protection from fire and theft).

body.text: Grounded Regulatory Analysis: During the T.D. 9786 comment process, commenters expressed concern that including inventory management, marketing, legal services, and government compliance services in G&A functions was overly broad because those functions often interact with external parties. The Treasury Department and the IRS retained those categories in § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B), clarifying that classification turns on whether the software is developed for internal G&A use or to enable third-party interaction. Routine customizations or integrations of Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) modules—such as transferring legacy financial, human resources, inventory, and sales data into a centralized enterprise-wide system, as illustrated in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(viii) Example 5—support G&A functions and are therefore classified as IUS, triggering the HTI test. Similarly, because "marketing" is explicitly listed as a G&A support service under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(3), software developed for a website intended solely for advertising/marketing purposes without allowing third parties to review data or initiate functions on the taxpayer's system is classified as IUS (Example 4 of the final regulations).
Exclusions and Upfront Exceptions from IUS: Software Subject to General R&D Rules

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(E) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6), software avoids the HTI test through two distinct legal pathways: (1) Upfront Exceptions (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii)), where the IUS rules of paragraph (c)(6) do not apply at all; and (2) Non-IUS Classification (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv)), where the software is not developed for use in G&A functions.
Upfront Statutory and Regulatory Exceptions (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii))

In finalizing T.D. 9786, the Treasury Department and the IRS restructured 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(i) and (ii) (Inapplicability of the high threshold of innovation test) so that paragraph (c)(6) explicitly does not apply to three categories of software:

items: Software Used in Qualified Research (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(E)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii)(A); Form 6765 Line 49(e) Category C.1): Software developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for internal use by the taxpayer for use in an activity that constitutes qualified research (other than the development of the internal use software itself)—such as software developed for use in a scientific laboratory or pilot research project.

Software Used in a Production Process (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(E)(ii) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii)(B); Form 6765 Line 49(e) Category C.2): Software developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for internal use by the taxpayer for use in a production process to which the requirements of section 41(d)(1) are met—such as automated manufacturing equipment controls or production-line quality inspection systems. (Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C), any plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component is treated as a separate business component from the product being produced.)

Combined Hardware-Software Packages (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii)(C); Form 6765 Line 49(e) Category C.3): A new or improved package of software and hardware developed together by the taxpayer as a single product (or the costs to modify an acquired software and hardware package), of which the software is an integral part, that is used directly by the taxpayer in providing services in its trade or business. In these cases, credit eligibility is determined by examining the combined hardware-software product as a single product under the general four-part test.

body.text: Non-IUS Categories: Commercial Sale and Third-Party Interaction (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv))

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv), software is not developed primarily for the taxpayer's internal use if it is not developed for use in G&A functions that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business. The regulation specifies two primary non-G&A exemplars. First, Commercial Sale, Lease, License, or Marketing (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv)(A); Form 6765 Line 49(e) Category D.1) covers software developed to be commercially sold, leased, licensed, or otherwise marketed to third parties, which includes cloud-based enterprise application or Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) platforms accessed online by customers (Example 9 of the final regulations), and which is never treated as Dual Function Software (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)) even if it also enables third-party interaction or data review. Second, Third-Party Interaction (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv)(B); Form 6765 Line 49(e) Category D.3) covers software developed to enable a taxpayer to interact with third parties or to allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system (without being used in any G&A function), such as customer-facing mobile or web banking, retail e-commerce, brokerage, or photograph-uploading applications (Example 8 of the final regulations, re-designated from Example 6 of the proposed regulations, where users upload and modify photographs at no charge while the taxpayer earns revenue by selling advertisements).

First, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(E), while "third party" generally means any corporation, trade or business, or other person not treated as a single taxpayer with the claimant under section 41(f), the regulation adds an explicit exclusion: "Additionally, for purposes of paragraph (c)(6)(iv)(B) of this section, third parties do not include any persons that use the software to support the general and administrative functions of the taxpayer." In 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(viii) Example 6 (Internal use software; definition of third party), taxpayer X develops software to interact electronically with its vendors and allow vendors to initiate functions or review data on X's system to improve X's inventory management. Because inventory management and procurement/accounts payable are G&A financial management functions (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(1)), the vendors are using the software to support X's G&A functions, are not considered "third parties" under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv)(B), and the software remains 100% Internal Use Software. Second, even where qualifying third parties (such as retail customers) are allowed to initiate functions or review data on a system that also performs G&A functions, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(A) does not pull the entire project out of IUS; rather, the software is classified as Dual Function Software (DFS) and is presumed to be IUS, requiring the taxpayer either to isolate the discrete third-party subset (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B)) or to satisfy the 25% safe harbor (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C)).
Divergence Between Financial Accounting (ASC 350-40 and ASU 2025-06) and Tax Law (IRC Section 174A, Section 174, and Section 41)

Currency Update on FASB ASU 2025-06 (Issued September 18, 2025) and IRC Section 174A (Enacted July 4, 2025): Additionally, under ASC 350-40-15-7, software developed internally for a specific R&D project or as a pilot project is excluded from ASC 350-40 and expensed as R&D under ASC 730.

On September 18, 2025, the FASB issued ASU 2025-06 (Targeted Improvements to the Accounting for Internal-Use Software), effective for annual reporting periods (fiscal years) beginning after December 15, 2027, including interim periods within those fiscal years (with early adoption permitted under prospective, modified, or retrospective transition methods). To accommodate modern iterative and agile software engineering, ASU 2025-06 eliminates all references to project stages in ASC 350-40 (and supersedes ASC 350-50, incorporating website development costs directly into ASC 350-40). Under amended ASC 350-40-25-12, an entity begins capitalizing eligible direct software costs only when both conditions are met: first, management, with the relevant authority, implicitly or explicitly authorizes and commits to funding the computer software project; and second, it is "probable" (defined in the FASB Master Glossary as "the future event or events are likely to occur") that the project will be completed and the software will be used to perform the function intended (the "probable-to-complete recognition threshold"). Crucially, under new ASC 350-40-25-12A, the probable-to-complete threshold is not met if "significant development uncertainty" exists, which occurs if either: (a) the software requires technological innovations or novel, unique, or unproven functions or features, and the uncertainty related to those elements has not been resolved through coding and testing; or (b) the significant performance requirements ("what an entity needs the software to do") have not been identified or continue to be substantially revised. Costs incurred prior to meeting the capitalization threshold, as well as training and data conversion costs (other than developing software to access or convert old data for new systems), must be expensed as incurred. Furthermore, ASU 2025-06 standardizes financial statement disclosures under ASC 360-10 (Property, Plant, and Equipment—Overall) for all capitalized software costs under ASC 350-40, while exempting them from intangible asset disclosures under ASC 350-30-50-1 through 50-3.

Analysis of the Inverse Relationship Between ASU 2025-06 and the Tax HTI Standard: Comparing ASU 2025-06 (ASC 350-40-25-12A) with 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii) reveals a structural inversion that tax and accounting teams must manage carefully. Under U.S. GAAP (ASC 350-40 as amended by ASU 2025-06), the scope of "internal-use software" is broad—encompassing any software acquired, internally developed, or modified solely to meet internal operational needs where there is no substantive plan to market it externally, including manufacturing robotics software, customer-facing banking portals, and vendor-hosted SaaS platforms where customers cannot take possession of the software without significant penalty (ASC 350-40-15-4A). However, if a project has unresolved technological uncertainty involving novel or unproven features (ASC 350-40-25-12A), GAAP capitalization is deferred (costs must be expensed) until coding and testing resolve that uncertainty. Conversely, under Federal Tax Law (26 U.S.C. § 41 and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)), the scope of "internal use software" is narrow (restricted strictly to the three G&A functions), and for G&A software to qualify for the § 41 R&D credit under the HTI test, "substantial uncertainty" due to technical risk must exist at the beginning of activities (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C)). Thus, the exact window where ASU 2025-06 prohibits GAAP capitalization due to unresolved novel technological uncertainty (ASC 350-40-25-12A) is the primary window where IRC § 41 HTI experimentation occurs, whereas routine ERP configurations capitalized under ASC 350-40 (once requirements are set and no novel uncertainty exists) generally fail the IRC § 41 HTI test. body.text: The Qualification Threshold: Analyzing the High-Threshold-of-Innovation (HTI) Test

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(i) (General rule), research with respect to software developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for the taxpayer's internal use is eligible for the IRC § 41 research credit only if: (A) the research with respect to the software satisfies the four-part requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1); (B) the research with respect to the software is not otherwise excluded under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4) (other than § 41(d)(4)(E))—such as research after commercial production (§ 41(d)(4)(A)), adaptation of an existing business component (§ 41(d)(4)(B)), reproduction of an existing business component, efficiency surveys or routine data collection/testing, foreign research (§ 41(d)(4)(F)), social sciences/arts/humanities, or funded research (§ 41(d)(4)(H)); and (C) the software satisfies the three-prong High-Threshold-of-Innovation (HTI) test of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii).
Component 1: The Innovative Requirement (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)(1) and (B))

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)(1) and (B), software is innovative if the software would result in a reduction in cost or improvement in speed or other measurable improvement, that is substantial and economically significant, if the development is or would have been successful. The regulation explicitly specifies that this is "a measurable objective standard, not a determination of the unique or novel nature of the software or the software development process". Furthermore, in the Preamble to T.D. 9786, in response to a commenter's concern that language in the proposed regulations stating it was "not always necessary" to have a revolutionary discovery could imply that a revolutionary discovery was sometimes required, the Treasury Department and the IRS removed that sentence and confirmed that a "revolutionary discovery" (such as creating a brand-new programming language, operating system, architecture, or algorithm) is not required to satisfy the HTI test. Nor must the development actually succeed, provided the intended improvement would have been substantial and economically significant if successful. Because 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(B) mandates a measurable, objective standard, taxpayers must establish quantitative performance baselines prior to development (e.g., existing transaction latency, server hardware expenditure, or manual processing labor hours) and document the projected substantial and economically significant improvement at the project's outset.
Component 2: The Significant Economic Risk Requirement (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)(2) and (C))

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)(2) and (C), software development involves significant economic risk if "the taxpayer commits substantial resources to the development and if there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that such resources would be recovered within a reasonable period." The regulatory text establishes three core legal principles governing this requirement: first, the term "substantial uncertainty" requires a higher level of uncertainty and technical risk than that required for business components that are not internal use software; second, this standard does not require technical uncertainty regarding whether the final result can ever be achieved, but rather whether the final result can be achieved within a timeframe that will allow the substantial resources committed to the development to be recovered within a reasonable period (which Section VII.B of the T.D. 9786 Preamble confirms is a case-by-case factual determination based on the taxpayer's specific facts and circumstances); and third, technical risk arises from uncertainty that is technological in nature (as defined in § 1.41-4(a)(4)), and substantial uncertainty must exist at the beginning of the taxpayer's activities.

Exact Regulatory Nuance on Design Uncertainty vs. Capability/Method Uncertainty: In the 2015 proposed regulations (REG-153656-03), the IRS had proposed restricting "substantial uncertainty" exclusively to uncertainty regarding capability or method, excluding appropriate design uncertainty. In T.D. 9786, commenters pointed out that capability, methodology, and design uncertainties are often inextricably linked and that delineating them creates administrative burdens. In response, the Treasury Department and the IRS removed the explicit reference to capability and method uncertainty from the text of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C), stating that the focus of the significant economic risk test should be on the overall level of uncertainty rather than classifying the types of uncertainty. However, the Preamble to T.D. 9786 (81 FR 68306, Section VII.A, Design Uncertainty) explicitly cautions taxpayers:

"While there may be design uncertainty in the development of internal use software, substantial uncertainty generally exists only when there is also uncertainty in regard to the capability or method of achieving the intended result. ... However, the Treasury Department and the IRS believe that internal use software research activities that involve only uncertainty related to appropriate design, and not capability or methodology, would rarely qualify as having substantial uncertainty for purposes of the high threshold of innovation test."

As illustrated in the regulatory conclusions to Example 16 and Example 18 (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(viii)), even if internal use software meets both the Innovative requirement ((c)(6)(vii)(A)(1)) and the Not Commercially Available requirement ((c)(6)(vii)(A)(3)), it fails the HTI test if the taxpayer's development activities did not involve substantial uncertainty due to technical risk that the committed resources would be recovered within a reasonable period. Specifically, in Example 18, taxpayer X, a multinational manufacturer, installs an ERP system running off a single database and builds interface software to integrate part of its legacy G&A system with the new ERP system across mutual incompatibilities. Although the integration would provide a substantial and economically significant reduction in cost and improvement in speed, no commercial application is available, and X is uncertain regarding the appropriate design of the interface software, X knows that given a reasonable period of time to experiment with various designs it will be able to determine the appropriate design and recover its substantial committed resources within a reasonable period—and therefore Example 18 concludes that X's activities fail the HTI test because they lack Significant Economic Risk under paragraph (c)(6)(vii)(A)(2).
Component 3: The Not Commercially Available Requirement (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)(3) and (D))

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)(3), the software must not be commercially available for use by the taxpayer, meaning that "the software cannot be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for the intended purpose without modifications that would satisfy the requirements of paragraphs (c)(6)(vii)(A)(1) and (2) of this section" (the Innovative and Significant Economic Risk requirements).
Additionally, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(D) (Application of high threshold of innovation test) imposes a strict standalone evaluation boundary:

"The high threshold of innovation test of paragraph (c)(6)(vii) of this section takes into account only the results anticipated to be attributable to the development of new or improved software at the beginning of the software development independent of the effect of any modifications to related hardware or other software. The implementation of existing technology by itself is not evidence of innovation, but the use of existing technology in new ways could be evidence of a high threshold of innovation if it resolves substantial uncertainty as defined in paragraph (c)(6)(vii)(C) of this section."
Table 3 summarizes the statutory and regulatory requirements of the three-part HTI test under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii).

cells: 1. Innovative (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)(1) & (B))

Software would result in a reduction in cost or improvement in speed or other measurable improvement, that is substantial and economically significant, if the development is or would have been successful.

Objective, measurable standard determined from anticipated software results alone (independent of hardware/other software changes); does not require a revolutionary discovery or ultimate project success.
2. Significant Economic Risk (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)(2) & (C))

Requires a higher degree of technical uncertainty at the beginning of activities than non-IUS components; design-only uncertainty (without capability or method uncertainty) rarely qualifies (Examples 16 and 18).

body.text: Regulatory Illustration (Example 17)

In 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(viii) Example 17 (Internal use software; application of the high threshold of innovation test), taxpayer X seeks to expand internal computing power for G&A computations without purchasing new hardware by developing a screen-saver-like application running on thousands of idle employee PCs and workstations that fetches and executes jobs from a central server until the job finishes or the employee resumes working on the computer. Because the software supports G&A computations and is not intended for commercial sale or third-party interaction, it is IUS. However, it satisfies the HTI test because: (1) avoiding new hardware purchases provides a substantial, economically significant cost reduction or speed improvement (Innovative); (2) at the outset, no commercial application existed with this capability (Not Commercially Available); and (3) X committed substantial resources while facing substantial technical uncertainty regarding the capability of developing a server application able to schedule and distribute jobs across thousands of PCs and workstations and handle all user machine error conditions within a reasonable recovery period (Significant Economic Risk).

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(3), "logistics" is explicitly classified as a G&A support service ("facility services (for example, grounds keeping, housekeeping, janitorial, and logistics)"). Accordingly, if used purely internally without third-party interaction, this hypothetical software is IUS and qualifies under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii) because it targets a measurable, economically significant 15% optimization improvement (Innovative), commits $2,000,000 in substantial capital at risk of non-recovery due to algorithmic capability uncertainty (Significant Economic Risk), and cannot be purchased off the shelf (Not Commercially Available).
Special Case Analysis: Dual Function Software (DFS) and the 25% Safe Harbor
Presumption of Internal Use and the Two-Step DFS Framework (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi))

Many modern enterprise systems are neither purely internal back-office tools nor purely external customer applications. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(A), software developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer both for use in G&A functions that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business and to enable a taxpayer to interact with third parties or to allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system is defined as Dual Function Software (DFS). By default, unless paragraph (c)(6)(vi)(B) or (C) applies, DFS is presumed to be developed primarily for a taxpayer's internal use.

However, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B) and (C) establish a sequential two-step relief mechanism that must be applied based on the taxpayer's intent and the facts and circumstances at the beginning of software development (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(D)). Under Step 1 — Identification of the Third-Party Subset (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B)), to the extent that a taxpayer can identify a discrete subset of elements of dual function software that only enables a taxpayer to interact with third parties or allows third parties to initiate functions or review data (the "third party subset"), the presumption of internal use under paragraph (c)(6)(vi)(A) does not apply to that third-party subset. Consequently, the third-party subset is treated as Non-IUS under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv)(B), and 100% of its allocable QREs are evaluated under the standard four-part test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) without regard to the HTI test.

Under Step 2 — The 25% Safe Harbor for Remaining Dual Function Software or Subset (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C)), if, after applying Step 1 (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B)), there remains dual function software or a subset of elements of dual function software (the "dual function subset") that performs both G&A and third-party functions and cannot be further separated, the taxpayer may include 25% of the qualified research expenditures of such remaining dual function software or dual function subset in computing the IRC § 41 credit without satisfying the HTI test, provided two mandatory conditions are met: first, the taxpayer's research activities related to the development or improvement of the dual function software or dual function subset constitute qualified research under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d) (without regard to § 41(d)(4)(E)) with allocable QREs under § 41(b); and second, the use of the dual function software or dual function subset by third parties (or by the taxpayer to interact with third parties) is reasonably anticipated to constitute at least 10% of the dual function software's or dual function subset's total use, estimated at the beginning of software development (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(D)) using an objective, reasonable method within the taxpayer's industry.

Objective Measurement Methods and the "No Stacking" Rule: Under the verbatim text of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C), an objective, reasonable method within the taxpayer's industry "may include, but is not limited to, processing time, amount of data transfer, and number of software user interface screens" (and the T.D. 9786 Preamble also notes the number of third-party initiated functions as an example mentioned in proposed guidance). Furthermore, as EY Tax Alert (2016-1704) and Form 6765 Instructions confirm, the safe harbor is optional rather than mandatory, and taxpayers cannot "stack" the safe harbor and the HTI test on the same dual function subset: a taxpayer electing the 25% safe harbor on a dual function subset foregoes claiming the remaining 75% of QREs for that subset under the HTI test. Conversely, if anticipated third-party use is less than 10% (as in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(viii) Example 13, where anticipated third-party use is 5%), the 25% safe harbor is inapplicable, and the dual function software can qualify only if it satisfies the full three-part HTI test under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii).
Step-by-Step Verification of the Regulatory DFS Examples (Examples 12, 13, and 14)

To illustrate the exact mathematical mechanics of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B) and (C), the regulations provide three linked hypothetical illustrations (Examples 12, 13, and 14 of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(viii)), each involving a taxpayer X that incurs $50,000 in total software research expenditures on Dual Function Software whose development otherwise satisfies the general four-part test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d) (without regard to § 41(d)(4)(E)) and § 41(b).

In Hypothetical Scenario 1 (Example 13 — Safe Harbor Inapplicable Due to <10% Anticipated Third-Party Use), X develops Dual Function Software costing $50,000 and is unable to identify a discrete third-party subset under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B). Using an objective, reasonable method at the beginning of development, X determines that third-party use to initiate functions is reasonably anticipated to constitute 5% of the software's total use. Because 5% is less than the minimum 10% usage threshold of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C), safe harbor QRE recovery is $0 (0% × $50,000 = $0). The entire $50,000 is presumed to be IUS under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(A) and can be included in computing the research credit only if the software satisfies all three prongs of the HTI test under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii).

In Hypothetical Scenario 2 (Example 12 — Unseparated DFS Qualifying for the 25% Safe Harbor), X undertakes the same $50,000 Dual Function Software project where no third-party subset can be isolated, except X determines at the outset using an objective, reasonable method that anticipated third-party use is 15% of total use. Because 15% meets or exceeds the 10% threshold (15% ≥ 10%), the safe harbor of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C) applies. Multiplying total allocable QREs by the 25% safe harbor rate ($50,000 × 25% = $12,500) allows X to include $12,500 (25% of $50,000) in computing its IRC § 41 credit without having to meet the HTI test, while the remaining $37,500 ($50,000 − $12,500) is excluded.

In Hypothetical Scenario 3 (Example 14 — Combining Third-Party Subset Isolation with the 25% Safe Harbor), X develops Dual Function Software with total research expenditures of $50,000, but under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B), X isolates a discrete third-party subset (Subset A) accounting for 50% ($25,000) of total expenditures. For the remaining dual function subset (Subset B, accounting for the other 50%, or $25,000), X determines at the beginning of development that third-party processing time is reasonably anticipated to account for 15% of Subset B's total processing time. Under Step 1 (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B)), Subset A is not presumed to be IUS, so 100% of Subset A's expenditures qualify under the standard four-part test ($50,000 × 50% × 100% = $25,000). Under Step 2 (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C)), because anticipated third-party processing time for Subset B is 15% (≥10%), Subset B qualifies for the 25% safe harbor ($25,000 × 25% = $6,250). Combining both subsets yields $25,000 + $6,250 = $31,250 (62.5% of $50,000) in eligible QREs under the standard four-part test—an increase of $18,750 (+150%) over the unseparated safe harbor in Example 12.
Establishing a Defensible IUS Compliance, Substantiation, and Reporting Framework

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d), taxpayers claiming the IRC § 41 research credit must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit. Furthermore, on redesigned IRS Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, Rev. January 2025, expanded from two pages to four pages) and its final instructions (Instructions for Form 6765, Rev. December 2025, released February 6, 2026), the IRS moved the IRC § 280C(c) reduced credit election (Item A) and controlled group / common control reporting (Item B) to the top of the form and introduced three new sections: Section E (Other Information), Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary), and Section G (Business Component Information). While Sections E and F are mandatory for all filers starting with 2024 and 2025 returns—requiring disclosure of the total number of business components generating QREs, officers' wages included in QREs, acquisitions or dispositions of a major portion of a trade or business, new categories of expenditures, and whether QREs were determined under the ASC 730 Directive (Line 41)—Section G is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 (unless filing an amended return) and becomes mandatory for all filers for tax years beginning after 2025, unless the taxpayer meets one of two explicit exceptions: (1) the taxpayer is a qualified small business (QSB) under section 41(h)(3) (defined under § 41(h)(1)–(2)) that checks the box to claim a reduced payroll tax credit; or (2) the taxpayer's total QREs determined at the controlled group level (Line 48) are equal to or less than $1.5 million, its average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years (under IRC § 448(c)(3) without regard to § 448(c)(3)(A)) are equal to or less than $50 million, and the taxpayer is reporting a research credit on an original return.

Under the "80%/Top 50" business components rule in Section G of Form 6765, taxpayers required to complete Section G must report component-by-component information in descending order by total QRE amount across Columns 49(a)–(f) and Columns 50–56 for a minimum of 80% of total QREs, up to a maximum of 50 business components, with any remaining components reported in aggregate by entering "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c) and the aggregate dollar amounts in Columns 50–56 (or entering "ASC 730 Directive" in Column 49(c) if Line 41 is checked "Yes"). Crucially, for every reported software business component, taxpayers must classify the software on Line 49(e) into one of the ten specific regulatory options shown in Table 4.

items: Preliminary Four-Tier Classification and Form 6765 Line 49(e) Mapping (Phase I): At project inception, classify every software development business component into Category A (IUS), Category B (DFS), Category C (Excepted from IUS treatment), or Category D (Non-IUS) in accordance with Table 4 and Form 6765 Section G Line 49(e), and embed the business component name or unique alphanumeric identifier (Column 49(c)) into general ledger entries and employee time-tracking systems.

Contemporaneous Intent Documentation (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(v)) (Phase I): Preserve inception-date project charters, product roadmaps, architectural specifications, and capital authorization requests demonstrating initial project purpose, because classification as IUS, Non-IUS, or DFS depends on the taxpayer's intent and the facts and circumstances at the beginning of software development (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(v) and (vi)(D)), and segregate any subsequent software improvements into separate business components evaluated according to their own inception-date intent.

Dual Function Subset Isolation and 10% Usage Forecasting (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B)–(E)) (Phase I): Map system architecture (microservices, APIs, user interface modules) at the outset of Dual Function Software projects to isolate the discrete third-party subset (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B)), and contemporaneously document an objective, reasonable industry forecast (using anticipated processing time, amount of data transfer, or number of software user interface screens) for the remaining dual function subset (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C)) showing at least 10% anticipated third-party use by true third parties rather than vendors supporting the taxpayer's own G&A functions (Example 6).

Documenting Substantial Technical Uncertainty and Refund Specificity (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C) and CCM 20214101F) (Phase II): For pure IUS projects (and DFS subsets not using the 25% safe harbor), record the process of experimentation (§ 1.41-4(a)(5)) and establish that substantial uncertainty regarding capability or methodology (not merely routine appropriate design choices, which Section VII.A of the T.D. 9786 Preamble and Example 18 note rarely qualify) existed at the beginning of activities. Additionally, when claiming a research credit refund on an amended return (where Form 6765 Section G Column 49(f) is required, and the IRS 45-day perfection period has been extended through January 10, 2027), satisfy IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F (issued Sept. 17, 2021; released Oct. 15, 2021) and 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1) within the 26 U.S.C. § 6511 limitations period (3 years from return filing or 2 years from tax payment) by specifying under penalties of perjury: (i) all business components, (ii) all research activities performed, (iii) all individuals performing each activity (or breaking out wages across actual conduct in Column 50, direct supervision in Column 51, and direct support in Column 52), (iv) the information each individual sought to discover (Column 49(f)), and (v) total qualified wage, supply, and contract expenses, with exact page citations to any attached study.

Quantifying Substantial and Economically Significant Improvements (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(B) & (D)) (Phase II): Establish pre-development quantitative baselines (cost, processing speed, throughput) and project the objective, measurable, substantial, and economically significant improvement attributable solely to the new or improved software, independent of any modifications to related hardware or other software (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(D)).

Substantiating Commercial Unavailability and Vendor Contract Rights/Risk (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)(3), § 1.41-2(e), and § 1.41-4A(d)) (Phase II): Document market gap analyses proving that no off-the-shelf software could be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for the intended purpose without modifications meeting the Innovative and Significant Economic Risk requirements (noting that vendor product evaluation itself is excluded from experimentation under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8) Example 5), and ensure all third-party contractor agreements (26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)) are executed prior to research performance, grant the taxpayer rights to the research results, place non-contingent financial risk on the taxpayer, and preserve the taxpayer's substantial rights under the funded research rules of 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d).

Applying IRS Software Audit Guidelines Accurately (I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and § 41(d)(4)) (Phase III): Use the IRS Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software for its actual administrative scope—screening out software activities rated by the IRS as "High Risk" of failing I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) across all software (specifically Maintenance of Existing Software Applications/Products, such as minor releases 1.1/1.2, corrective debugging, security patches, and perfective enhancements; Software Application Configuration of vendor-purchased packages; rewriting an application in a new language; writing hardware device drivers from vendor specifications; data quality/cleansing/consistency formatting; and bundling existing individual software products into suites, as well as post-production debugging under § 41(d)(4)(A) and customer adaptation under § 41(d)(4)(B))—while recognizing that the Audit Guidelines explicitly do not address the IUS exclusion under § 41(d)(4)(E).

Reconciling GAAP (ASC 350-40 / ASU 2025-06) and Tax (IRC § 174A / § 174 and IRC § 41) Cost Pools (Phase III): Maintain a formal accounting bridge reconciling software costs capitalized or expensed under U.S. GAAP (ASC 350-40, including costs expensed prior to resolving "significant development uncertainty" under ASU 2025-06 ASC 350-40-25-12A or expensed under ASC 730 via ASC 350-40-15-7) with domestic R&E expenditures deducted under 26 U.S.C. § 174A (including any 2025/2026 transition deductions for unamortized 2022–2024 domestic R&E under OBBBA), foreign R&E amortized over 15 years under § 174 (excluded from § 41 under § 41(d)(4)(F)), and domestic QREs claimed on Form 6765 (including the 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c) election on Item A).

Annual Multi-Year Project Review and Recalibration (Phase IV): Audit ongoing multi-year software projects annually to verify whether functional pivots—such as adding G&A modules to a commercial product or adding third-party portals to an internal G&A system—have created a separate improvement business component under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(v) or altered anticipated third-party usage relative to the 10% DFS safe harbor threshold.

Pre-Development Specialist Consultation (Phase IV): Engage R&D tax credit specialists alongside software architects at project initiation so that inception-date intent (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(v)), third-party subset boundaries (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B)), and HTI technical baselines (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)) are captured contemporaneously during engineering sprints rather than reconstructed retroactively during an IRS examination.
